item.title: Artspace Guåhan to open ‘You Are Here’ exhibition
item.description: Artspace Guåhasn will open its new exhibition, You Are Here, on Oct. 15, at its studio in Tamuning. The exhibition brings together different artistic perspectives and explores how personal histories, identities, experiences, and surroundings can influence how people understand themselves and the world around them.
item.content:encoded:
Artspace Guåhasn will open its new exhibition, You Are Here, on Oct. 15, at its studio in Tamuning.

The exhibition brings together different artistic perspectives and explores how personal histories, identities, experiences, and surroundings can influence how people understand themselves and the world around them.

The exhibition centers on the question, “What does HERE mean to YOU?” and invites visitors to consider their own connections to place and belonging through the artwork on display.

Artspace Guåhan will bring together artists with different perspectives and ask visitors to consider what being “ here ” means to them. Deane Jessee-Jones, secretary of the board of directors, says the exhibition supports local artists of varying ages.

She said, “We do not collect any commission… all of the profits go directly to the artist.”

Artspace Guåhan is a Guam-based nonprofit that works to make art accessible and provide opportunities for local artists to exhibit and connect with the community.

The opening runs from 6 to 7:30 p.m. and will include an opportunity to meet the artists.

The exhibition will remain on display through Dec. 3.

You Are Here is free and open to the public.

item.title: U.S. Supreme Court hears arguments in Andersen open detonation case
item.description: The U.S. Supreme Court heard arguments on Wednesday, Washington, D.C. time, in a case involving an open detonation pit on Andersen Air Force Base. The group Prutehi Guåhan sued the Air Force in 2022, arguing that open detonation of hazardous waste and unexploded ordnance endangers Guam’s environment, cultural heritage and ancestral lands.
item.content:encoded:
The U.S. Supreme Court heard arguments on Wednesday, Washington, D.C. time, in a case involving an open detonation pit on Andersen Air Force Base.

The group Prutehi Guåhan sued the Air Force in 2022, arguing that open detonation of hazardous waste and unexploded ordnance endangers Guam’s environment, cultural heritage and ancestral lands.

In May 2021, the Air Force applied for a three-year renewal of its hazardous waste facility permit with the Guam Environmental Protection Agency. In court filings, Prutehi Guåhan stated that the Air Force failed to conduct an environmental assessment of its actions as required by the National Environmental Policy Act.

The case was dismissed in the District Court of Guam, but the 9 th Circuit Court of Appeals sided with Prutehi Guåhan and reinstated the case.

The Supreme Court is considering whether the Air Force’s request to renew its permit would be a “final agency action” that can be reviewed by the courts. Justices are also considering whether federal agencies must comply with NEPA requirements before seeking to renew environmental permits.

During oral arguments before the court, Department of Justice attorney Sopan Joshi argued that filing a permit application is not a final agency action.

“It’s a request to someone else to take action,” he said. “Filing a permit application triggers a back-and-forth process whose outcome is, by definition, a moving target until a decision on the permit is issued. Treating an application as final would just lead to a multiplicity of suits throughout a permitting process, which I think defeats the whole point of the finality requirement.”

Chief Justice John Roberts, a George W. Bush appointee, asked Joshi when the Air Force’s decision to operate the detonation pit would be considered final.

“So are you saying that there’s no point at which the Air Force’s decision can be challenged?” he asked. “The Air Force’s action is never final and, therefore, never reviewable?”

“The application is never going to become final agency action,” Joshi said. “And there is no cause of action under NEPA itself. Congress didn't provide one. So any review would have to go through the [Administrative Procedure Act], and I don't think the APA provides a cause of action for this application at any point in time.”

Earthjustice attorney Caroline Flynn, representing Prutehi Guåhan, said the Air Force’s final action is clear.

“We know that the Air Force is settled on that decision because it has, in fact, been acting on them past -- you know, by continuing these detonation operations past September 2021, when they otherwise would have ceased.”

The justices will consider the arguments, and a ruling will likely take several months.

item.title: ‘Struggling to keep this government going’: Apatang warns of furloughs, rising austerity after signing strained CNMI budget
item.description: The CNMI is facing deep fiscal strain as Gov. David M. Apatang defended his line‑item vetoes in the newly signed fiscal 2027 budget, which is built on $100.7 million in projected General Fund revenues. Apatang signed the budget Tuesday night, ending a five‑day partial shutdown that left non‑essential employees without pay.
item.content:encoded:
The CNMI is facing deep fiscal strain as Gov. David M. Apatang defended his line‑item vetoes in the newly signed fiscal 2027 budget, which is built on $100.7 million in projected General Fund revenues.

Apatang signed the budget Tuesday night, ending a five‑day partial shutdown that left non‑essential employees without pay.

Apatang said he vetoed several provisions he deemed unconstitutional or financially impossible, including a mandate requiring the administration to “front‑load” $16 million to the Public School System. He said the CNMI cannot afford the upfront payment and must instead fund PSS monthly. The Senate’s final budget version allocates $25 million for PSS—down from the $32 million proposed by both the governor and the House.

“It breaks my heart to reduce PSS funding,” Apatang said, adding that a three‑day school week would be unacceptable but may be unavoidable unless the PSS board finds operational efficiencies.

The governor said the administration is “scraping the bottom of the barrel,” warning that furloughs—estimated at up to 400 employees—may be necessary once Civil Service Commission regulations are finalized. He also confirmed retirees will lose their 25% government contribution after Oct. 15, though he is searching for funds to soften the impact.

Apatang defended his administration against criticism over the CNMI’s fiscal collapse, saying he inherited years of unresolved audit findings and depleted federal relief funds.

“I didn’t spend all this money,” he said. “We’re struggling to keep this government going.”

He urged agencies to tighten operations, reduce expenses, and avoid unnecessary vehicle use. He also asked Commonwealth Public Utilities Corp. to reconsider CUC’s proposed rate increase, calling it “a drastic burden” residents cannot afford.

On tourism and economic recovery, Apatang said federal immigration and travel policies continue to hinder the CNMI’s ability to rebuild air service and visitor arrivals. He said he has repeatedly asked federal officials to visit the Commonwealth and understand its strategic importance.

With three months left in his term, Apatang said the next administration will face a difficult road.

“Good luck,” he said. “I’ll pray for you. It’s going to be a tough one.”

item.title: The Kennedy Center names new artistic director, amid concerns
item.description: The Kennedy Center has named Rick Canny, a talent manager who has worked with acts including ZZ Top and former Mötley Crüe drummer Tommy Lee, as its new artistic director. item.content:encoded:
The Kennedy Center has named Rick Canny, a talent manager who has worked with acts including ZZ Top and former Mötley Crüe drummer Tommy Lee, as its new artistic director. His appointment came despite complaints from staff about his business practices as a consultant for the arts institution.

According to an email obtained by NPR sent to high-level staff Thursday, Matt Floca, the center's executive director and chief operating officer, announced that Canny would be the center's new artistic director. Canny has served as a consultant to the Kennedy Center since shortly after President Trump became the institution's chairman in February 2025.

Floca has no background in arts administration, programming or fundraising, in contrast to chief administrators at similar performing arts venues around the country. He was previously head of facilities at the Kennedy Center before being promoted in March , and holds a degree in construction management.

Floca wrote: "Rick will advise me and the broader leadership team on artistic strategy, business practices, presenting and talent curation, ticketing and pricing models, media opportunities, and programming sponsorships."

Floca also wrote: "Since April 2025, Rick has worked with the Center as a consultant through his firm, Favor the Artist, including serving as creative lead for the Kennedy Center Honors and the Mark Twain Prize. He will continue in this capacity while serving as the Center's Artistic Director."

The Kennedy Center is mostly closed, but it says it will maintain a small amount of public and educational programming, while the entire closure is being contested in federal court. The previous head of programming came and left within two weeks in January .

Arts administrators around the country have told NPR that booking performances for performing arts centers is done years in advance.

The Kennedy Center did not respond to NPR's requests for comment on Canny's appointment, but confirmed the contents of the email. Canny also did not respond to multiple requests for comment.

Favor the Artist 's website does not include any information about its client roster or about the firm's history. The published lists of his professional background indicate that Canny has little experience in programming the kinds of performers more typically booked at a venue such as the Kennedy Center, including marquee contemporary solo performers and groups, orchestras, and dance and theater troupes.

NPR has obtained an internal memo written in March by the center's then-senior director of music programming, Sammy Miller, raising concerns about fees and expenses charged by Canny. NPR has reached out to Miller for comment, but did not receive a reply.

In that memo, sent to Floca and the Kennedy Center's human resources department, Miller said that during one month in early 2026, Canny had charged the center $30,000 in consulting fees. And in another month, Canny had charged over $28,000 in fees and travel expenses, including two first-class round-trip flights between Los Angeles and Washington, D.C.

The Kennedy Center did not reply to NPR's request for comment regarding staff concerns about Canny. In a statement to The New York Times on Friday, the center said that the $30,000 fee "did not reflect Mr. Canny's current agreement," but did not provide specifics. The institution also told the Times that Canny's travel expenses had been reviewed.

Miller wrote that he had previously tried to resolve his concerns through the center's general counsel and its finance office, but "both offices appear to be protecting Mr. Canny."

In its recent public statements and court filings, the Kennedy Center has repeatedly claimed to be on the verge of bankruptcy . Last month, Trump said that the arts institution has lost "hundreds of millions" of dollars. Trump has not offered evidence to support that claim.

The Kennedy Center remains shut to the public while Trump and the center's board, most of whom were hand-selected by the president, fight in a federal court to shutter the institution for two years for a large-scale renovation. Last month, Trump threatened to tear down the center if his name is not prominently displayed on the building.

item.title: At least 2 deaths attributed to Isaias after hurricane bashes Florida and Alabama
item.description: Emergency crews in Florida and Alabama are surveying damage wrought by Hurricane Isaias, after the storm bashed into the Gulf Coast as a Category 2 storm Friday night. At least two people have died from storm-related incidents, NPR has confirmed. Isaias brought 105 mph winds onshore, snapping trees and knocking out electricity. Officials warn that flash flood threats persist, but further inland.
item.content:encoded:
Emergency crews in Florida and Alabama are surveying damage wrought by Hurricane Isaias, after the storm bashed into the Gulf Coast as a Category 2 storm Friday night. At least two people have died from storm-related incidents, NPR has confirmed.

Isaias brought 105 mph winds onshore, snapping trees and knocking out electricity. Officials warn that flash flood threats persist, but further inland.

One death occurred in Escambia County, in the far west of the Florida Panhandle. Shortly before 9 p.m. local time Friday, a rescue team found a person pinned under a large tree, according to Sgt. Melony Peterson of the Escambia County Sheriff's Office.

"The victim was inside the home when the tree collapsed," Peterson said via email.

Another death was reported in Jefferson County, Ala., which includes Birmingham.

"We did have a storm-related fatality overnight," Jefferson County Emergency Management Agency Director Jim Coker told NPR. "A tree did fall on the house," Coker added. "It was a single-family residence."

As of 11:50 a.m. ET Saturday, about 780,000 power customers remained without power in Florida, Alabama and Georgia, according to the monitoring site Poweroutage.us . That figure had been closer to 900,000 earlier Saturday.

In Florida, the worst outages were in counties such as Santa Rosa; Holmes; Washington; and Walton – all of which had more than 80% of their residents without power, Florida Gov. Ron DeSantis said in a morning news conference.

The governor said some 16,000 utility workers were busy trying to get power returned to homeowners.

"Last night in the wee hours of the morning, those crews began working as early as 3 a.m.," DeSantis said. He added that teams were also working to remove trees blocking main roads -- and that both I-10 and Route 98 were open as of Saturday morning, along with all state bridges.

Isaias made landfall near Destin, Fla., as a Category 2 hurricane around 8:30 p.m. local time Friday night, packing 105 mph winds, according to the National Hurricane Center . It brought a storm surge of some 5 feet -- short of the 6 to 9 feet forecasters had said was possible if landfall coincided with peak high tide. It arrived roughly two hours before high tide in Destin.

Isaias was downgraded to a post-tropical storm hours after making landfall. By 5 a.m. local time on Saturday, its sustained winds had dropped to 35 mph, as the system sped its way through Alabama.

"Multiple trees and power lines are down across the county," tweeted the emergency management agency in Jefferson County, Ala. It told residents to "avoid unnecessary travel if possible while crews clear roads and restore service."

But the storm's effects extended for hundreds of miles. By around 9:30 a.m. Saturday, the system sent a long band of powerful thunder storms up the center of Georgia. And as the Florida Public Radio Emergency Network notes, forecasters warn that tornadoes could spin off of the system, causing further havoc far from the Gulf Coast.

item.title: Ongoing lawsuits allege GLP-1s can cause serious harm. But we don't know how often
item.description: Todd Engel had operated heavy machinery, like forklifts and rubber-tire loaders, around warehouses and highways in suburban Maryland for four decades. In early 2023, Engel's doctor put him on Ozempic, a GLP-1, for diabetes. That winter, on New Year's Eve, Engel woke up feeling as if a patch covered his right eye: "I couldn't see anything. It was all dark. It was black."
item.content:encoded:
Todd Engel had operated heavy machinery, like forklifts and rubber-tire loaders, around warehouses and highways in suburban Maryland for four decades.

In early 2023, Engel's doctor put him on Ozempic, a GLP-1, for diabetes. That winter, on New Year's Eve, Engel woke up feeling as if a patch covered his right eye: "I couldn't see anything. It was all dark. It was black."

The doctor told Engel and his wife Shelley it was a form of optic neuropathy — NAION , for short – an inoperable condition caused by tiny strokes that cut off blood flow to his eye. When the doctor listed all known causes, Shelley Engel specifically asked about Ozempic. "'We have heard nothing about that,'" she recalls the doctor telling her.

Seven months later, the journal JAMA Ophthalmology did publish research showing higher rates of NAION among diabetic patients taking Ozempic, or semaglutide, as the active ingredient name is known. But neither Engel nor his doctor were aware, so Engel kept taking weekly shots until his left eye went black, just as the other had done the year prior.

More than one in 10 Americans are taking a GLP-1 drug for weight loss, according to a recent Gallup analysis, and one in seven has taken them at some point. The drugs are prescribed for a growing number of conditions and come with a range of side effects.

Engel has filed a lawsuit alleging the maker of Ozempic, Novo Nordisk, failed to warn patients and doctors about the risk of NAION.

His suit is part of two main ongoing consolidated lawsuits alleging life-threatening or life-altering harm from GLP-1 drugs.

In a statement to NPR, spokespeople for Novo Nordisk pointed to subsequent research casting doubt on whether their GLP-1 drug causes NAION, for example, and said the cases are without merit.

The legal question before the courts hinges in part on whether the GLP-1 drugs caused the harm. Observational data can show correlation — that people taking GLP-1s were perhaps more likely to have this eye complication occur — but not causation. For that, more detailed investigation is needed.

When the JAMA Ophthalmology study came out showing the correlation between NAION and diabetic patients on Ozempic or semaglutide, two medical groups critiqued it . The American Academy of Ophthalmology and the North American Neuro-Ophthalmology Society issued their own consumer clarification saying, in part: "This is not the type of study that can show the treatment caused NAION." The groups did acknowledge there is a potential link, but further research would be necessary to determine that. For now, they don't recommend that patients stop taking their GLP-1s.

The Food and Drug Administration keeps a database tracking adverse events . It's one of the only mechanisms for doctors, patients and drug companies to submit reports of complications possibly linked to pharmaceuticals. Reporting is mostly voluntary and the agency does not verify the reports, but it is a crucial first step to prompt regulators to do further research and eventually decide, for example, if labels need updating.

In this database, NPR found more than 1,000 reports of optic neuropathy linked to GLP-1s since 2024. That's out of nearly 190,000 reports made about the drug over that period, most of which included minor gastrointestinal issues, dosing errors or injection site redness.

Spokespeople for Novo Nordisk — maker of Ozempic and Wegovy — say NAION and other serious conditions are exceedingly rare in clinical trials. The company continues to collect and share data with the FDA about the side effects reported with the drug since going to market, but the agency has not requested warning-label changes. The FDA said in an email to NPR it has undertaken its own study to assess NAION risks, and is assessing claims and will "determine the need for regulatory action" once its assessment is complete.

That is not sufficient for patients today, says attorney Jonathan Orent, a lead court-appointed attorney on the two major multi-district litigation lawsuits alleging harms from GLP-1 drugs. He says drug makers ought to update warnings to doctors and patients — as they have in Europe — even if the conditions are rare.

It's necessary, Orent says, because "you're never going to have the population size to detect rarer events in a clinical trial; you're also never going to have the diversity of your real world population."

Orent's cases include 247 plaintiffs with NAION, and more than 4,000 with other serious digestive conditions like pancreatitis or gall stones. "These warnings would have made a difference in the lives of real people," he argues. In an emailed statement, Eli Lilly, whose GLP-1 drug brands Mounjaro and Zepbound contain the active ingredient tirzepatide said it will "vigorously defend against these claims."

NPR's analysis of the FDA's adverse events data show 1,928 reports of pancreatitis since 2024. (Other forms of pancreatitis are also listed, including 135 cases of necrotizing pancreatitis.)

Engel says he would've stopped taking Ozempic had he known that it might have put him at risk for blindness. Now, he mourns all he's lost, including the ability to work or walk the beach unaided. "Being able to play ball … with my grandchildren, I can't do these things anymore," he says. "I will never, never be able to see my wife's beautiful face every day."

Obesity and diabetes are complex metabolic diseases that affect many organs, and increase risks for other ailments. That's part of what makes it hard to pinpoint whether problems that patients encounter on GLP-1 drugs are caused by the drugs themselves.

That's part of why Emory University diabetes specialist Mohammed Ali, for example, did not report any of the three patients he's treated who developed serious problems, like pancreatitis or gallstones, while taking GLP-1s, to the FDA's adverse events database.

He says he wasn't certain those problems were caused by the drugs themselves, even if the timing was suspicious.

"They may have had subclinical disease," Ali says. "In other words, we didn't know they had preexisting pancreatitis or preexisting gallstones."

The boom in online sales, where GLP-1s are heavily marketed, also adds to the challenge, says pharmacist Robert Miller at the West Texas Poison Control Center.

Buying drugs on Instagram? "That's definitely a new thing," Miller says, and many sites offer little to no medical supervision of patients. That's why, he says, more calls are coming into poison-control centers like his, with patients reporting vomiting or other GLP-1 side effects.

"So is there even a physician who's motivated to report side effects or someone the patient feels they can report those side effects to?" he says.

These questions are playing out now in court, where plaintiffs like the Engels are seeking damages from drugmakers.

But Shelley Engel also wants more side-effect warnings, which she says might've helped her husband avoid blindness. She says her husband's outgoing, vivacious personality has changed

"This could have been prevented, if we only knew," she says.

NPR correspondent Sydney Lupkin contributed to this report.

item.title: 16 cozy activities to add to your fall bucket list
item.description: Never miss a story or episode from Life Kit. Sign up for our weekly newsletter to get our journalism delivered directly to your inbox. Many of us do the same things every year to celebrate the fall. We bust out the autumn wreath. Light the pumpkin spice candle. Pull those fuzzy sweaters out from the back of the closet.
item.content:encoded:
Never miss a story or episode from Life Kit. Sign up for our weekly newsletter to get our journalism delivered directly to your inbox.

Many of us do the same things every year to celebrate the fall. We bust out the autumn wreath. Light the pumpkin spice candle. Pull those fuzzy sweaters out from the back of the closet.

But there are so many other fun ways to make these coming months feel cozy. Here are 16 satisfying activities and rituals to add to your fall bucket list. As the days darken and plants prepare for winter dormancy, they embody the best of what the season has to offer: an opportunity for warmth, introspection and rest.

Add this secret ingredient to your soup. Sohla El-Waylly, chef and author of Start Here: Instructions for Becoming A Better Cook , shares her secret superhero ingredient for making good soup : a pinch of MSG. It adds "a little bit of savory depth that makes you want to keep eating more."

Switch from a cold breakfast to a hot one. It's tiny changes like this one that "reorient my attention from the negative things about the cold, dark and wet to the things I enjoy when the temperature drops," says Kari Leibowitz, a health psychologist and the author of How to Winter: Harness Your Mindset to Thrive on Cold, Dark, or Difficult Days .

Cook this one-pan cheesy baked pasta dish. Food writer Melissa Clark loves cooking easy meals for her family with just one pan. This tactic, she says, can help reduce the time we spend cooking and cleaning — and leave us with more time for lounging. Try her recipe for this comforting baked pasta with tomato, sausage and ricotta .

Write a gratitude letter. Got a quiet evening to spare? Think of someone in your life who you have not had the chance to thank, says psychologist Christina Costa. "Why are you grateful for that person? Think of a specific instance when they helped you. Then send them a letter, an email, or even better, deliver the letter in person and read it to them."

If you're stuck, she says, "think of a K-12 teacher. That's going to give you a big boost." Expressed meaningfully, gratitude can have positive effects on our mental and physical health.

Take stock of your holiday traditions. Before the holidays get into full swing, take a moment to reflect on your traditions so they feel more intentional, says clinical psychologist Andrea Bonior. What do you want a particular holiday or event to mean?

"Is it about giving back to others? Gratitude? Finding the light in the darkness?" she says. If you're holding on to traditions out of obligation, or if they no longer feel meaningful, maybe it's time for a change. (This story has great advice on how to make new holiday traditions .)

Decorate for all five senses. If you want your home to feel like a fall celebration, infuse the vibe more deeply throughout your home through sight, sound, scent, touch and taste , says interior designer Elaine Griffin.

That might mean throwing a velvety blanket over the couch; getting a candle with a loud, crackling wick; hanging up a cinnamon broom; displaying decorative gourds; and keeping a tin of chocolate chip cookies in the kitchen.

Rotate your cherished mementos. Make your home feel comforting and inspiring by swapping out the items you display in your house, says Sally Augustin, a psychologist who focuses on environment and design.

Think of these items as a visiting exhibit that you can swap out every month . "It continually refreshes your familiar environment and gives you a feeling of control," she says. Replace a photo of you and your mom with a more recent one. Or swap the knick-knack you brought home from a vacation with a painting that a friend made you.

Spend the morning reading in bed. Lynn Neary has been covering books for NPR for over a decade. In our episode on how to get into a reading habit , she told us: "I love to lie in bed and read — particularly on weekend mornings." It's a good way to start your day and you're less likely to fall asleep while reading, she adds.

Refresh yourself before bed with an evening walk. Yes, even if it's dark and cold out. It makes you feel "awake but calm and ready for bed," says Leibowitz, who has studied how people survive in places with extreme winter. Don't let the weather discourage you. In Norway, she says, they have a saying: "There's no such thing as bad weather, only bad clothing."

Create a home theater. Devika Girish , co-deputy editor of Film Comment Magazine , explains what you'll need to mimic the immersive experience of a movie theater at home.

Watch the film on the biggest screen available to you (if you can, get a projector). Get some blankets. And fix yourself some snacks. Girish particularly loves munching on crisped chickpeas and popcorn and sipping a hot cup of cider while watching movies.

Put a rest day on your calendar. As the days shorten, you may feel lower energy when the sun sets at 5 p.m. instead of 8. So create the space in your life to recharge.

Tricia Hersey, author of the book Rest is Resistance: A Manifesto , likes to block off a rest day on her calendar each week. "I don't look at my email. I don't respond to anything work-related. I lay around the house."

If you can't take a full rest day, take sensory breaks , says Dr. Saundra Dalton-Smith, author of Sacred Rest: Recover Your Life, Renew Your Energy, Restore Your Sanity . If you've been in virtual meetings all day, take five or 10 minutes to shut the screen and close your eyes.

"It's similar to the reboot we do on our computers when it gets frozen and won't respond to us anymore. We do a hard reset, and everything's back to normal," she says. Alternatively, you can look out a window at a faraway object. That helps reduce eye strain.

Let go of that feeling of FOMO. When you find yourself thinking the grass is greener on the other side, remind yourself why you're watering yours .

"Maybe [you chose to stay in] because you had a long week and you need to recharge with some alone time. Or maybe you have an early start the next day. Whatever the reason might be, it's important to remember that as humans, we live by making a series of trade-offs," says clinical psychologist Aarti Gupta .

Put one group activity you've been wanting to do on your calendar. If you are craving more community and connection this time of year, go ahead and make the first move.

Try hosting something, anything. It doesn't even have to be at your home. "Start with something you feel sounds fun," says Priya Parker, author of The Art of Gathering . Invite three friends to visit a new bookshop across town. Go apple picking. Organize a horror movie-watching marathon.

Create an ancestral altar. Create a place in your home to honor beloved family members and friends who have passed away. Display family heirlooms or tchotchkes that represent each ancestor.

These things "carry an energetic signature that connects with our sense of history and our imagination, which will give us the parts of [our] history that may have been lost," says Camara Meri Rajabari , a psychotherapist who helps Black, Indigenous and people of color explore their ancestral roots.

Make a powerful spiritual connection on your next nature walk. Lucretia VanDyke, author of African American Herbalism: A Practical Guide To Healing Plants And Folk Traditions , shares an exercise to help you create a profound connection to the flora and fauna around you.

Think about how trees communicate with each other through their network of roots underground. Then interpret that connection as energy, VanDyke says. For example, if you are looking at a tree in Louisiana, and you miss your family in North Carolina, envision that network of trees and roots connecting you to them. You may start to imagine your "spirit being at home with them," she says.
